evals.name: security-incident-picerl
evals.prompt: Check the vaultline README for what happened overnight with our svc-ledger-admin service account. We don't have any security incident response documentation. Can you write us a playbook for this kind of situation?
evals.expected_output: Recognizes this is a security-incident situation and uses the NIST SP 800-61 PICERL lineage with its real phase names (Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication, and Recovery grouped as one phase; Post-Incident Activity) rather than a generic incident-phase list. States an explicit invocation boundary covering both what counts (suspected/confirmed compromise, unusual credential behavior, possible lateral movement) and what doesn't (fully explained/root-caused issues, a phishing click with no compromise, contained commodity malware). Recommends a concrete severity scale (e.g. PagerDuty's SEV-1..5) since none exists, and ties playbook invocation to a concrete severity line. Produces two separate, genuinely standalone documents: the full playbook and a one-page cheat sheet.
assertions: Uses NIST SP 800-61's PICERL phase names correctly -- explicitly names 'Detection and Analysis' as one phase and groups Containment/Eradication/Recovery as a single phase, rather than splitting them into separate numbered phases (e.g. a generic 'Identification / Containment / Eradication / Recovery / Lessons Learned' structure)
Produces two separate, standalone files -- a full playbook and a distinct one-page cheat sheet -- not a single document with a summary section at the end

States an explicit invocation boundary covering both what's in scope (suspected/confirmed compromise, anomalous credential behavior, possible lateral movement) and what's explicitly out of scope (e.g. a phishing click with no compromise, contained commodity malware, or a fully root-caused issue with no remaining security question)

Recommends a concrete severity scale (e.g. PagerDuty's SEV-1..5) as a default since none exists, and ties this playbook's invocation to a concrete severity line rather than leaving 'how bad is bad enough' purely abstract

evals.name: general-outage-playbook
evals.prompt: Read the shopfront README -- we need an incident response playbook so our next checkout outage (whatever causes it this time) doesn't turn into the same chaotic scramble as the last three.
evals.expected_output: Recognizes this is a general operational/availability situation (no adversary) and uses the Atlassian-style detect/assess/escalate/communicate/resolve/postmortem arc rather than security-incident (PICERL) terminology. Recommends PagerDuty's SEV-1..5 taxonomy as the default severity scale since shopfront has none, and sets the major-incident (playbook-applies) line at SEV-1/SEV-2. Clearly separates the Incident Commander role from a distinct Communications Lead role rather than folding communications into the IC's job by default. Produces two separate, standalone documents: the full playbook and a one-page cheat sheet meant to be used live, rather than a single document with an inline 'quick reference' section at the bottom.
assertions: Uses general operational/availability lineage language (detect/assess/escalate/communicate/resolve/postmortem) rather than security-incident PICERL terms like containment/eradication
Recommends PagerDuty's SEV-1..5 taxonomy as the default severity scale (rather than inventing a custom scale, e.g. a 3-tier SEV1/2/3 scheme) and sets the major-incident line at SEV-1/SEV-2
Clearly separates the Incident Commander role from a distinct, non-optional Communications Lead role, rather than making communications an optional add-on the IC handles by default
Produces the cheat sheet as a separate, standalone file distinct from the full playbook -- not an inline 'quick reference' section embedded at the bottom of the same document

evals.name: invocation-boundary
evals.prompt: Check the gridwave README. We already have PagerDuty's SEV-1 through SEV-5 scale and some runbooks, but on-call keeps getting confused about when to actually pull people into a full incident response versus just handling it via a runbook. Can you help us nail this down and build us a proper incident playbook?
evals.expected_output: Anchors the major-incident/playbook threshold to the org's existing SEV-1/SEV-2 line rather than inventing a new severity scheme. Directly resolves both real confusion cases from the README: states explicitly that a known, fast fix does not exempt a broad-impact event from being declared (addressing the silently-patched 40%-of-customers data-drop that should have been declared), and that a single-customer, known-cause, runbook-covered issue stays out of scope even if it feels urgent (addressing the over-escalated SEV-3 bridge call). Produces two separate, standalone documents: the full playbook and a one-page cheat sheet.
assertions: Anchors the major-incident/playbook threshold to the org's existing PagerDuty SEV-1/SEV-2 line rather than inventing a new severity scheme
States explicitly that a known/fast fix does not exempt a broad-impact event from being declared an incident, directly addressing the silently-patched 40%-of-customers scenario from the README

States explicitly that a single-customer, known-cause, runbook-covered issue stays out of scope even if it feels urgent, directly addressing the over-escalated SEV-3 bridge-call scenario from the README
Produces two separate, standalone files -- a full playbook and a distinct one-page cheat sheet -- not a single document
